source_item.title: U.S. bond sell-off deepens as energy shock and trade friction lock in hawkish Fed

card.plain_headline: US bond prices fall as inflation fears and hawkish Fed persist
card.what_happened: US government bonds are experiencing a significant sell-off, meaning their prices are falling and yields are rising. This is driven by persistent inflation concerns, particularly from energy prices, and expectations that the Federal Reserve will maintain a hawkish (tightening) monetary policy.
card.what_happened_verbose: The market for US Treasury bonds is seeing a sharp decline in prices, which translates to a rise in their yields (interest rates). This 'bond sell-off' is being fueled by two main factors: an 'energy shock' (rising oil and gas prices contributing to inflation) and the expectation that the Federal Reserve will remain 'hawkish.' A hawkish Fed is one that prioritizes fighting inflation, even if it means keeping interest rates higher for longer, which makes existing bonds with lower yields less attractive.

affected.reason: Ultra-short term bonds are less sensitive to rate hikes than longer-duration bonds, but rising rates generally increase short-term yields.
